FOREWORD
Despite the unprecedented challenges of recent years — the COVID-19 pandemic, global economic 
turbulence, and the intensifying impacts of climate change — Uzbekistan’s unwavering partnership with the 
United Nations and other international allies has remained a cornerstone of our progress. 
Together, we have strengthened our resilience, advanced our economic transformation, and safeguarded 
the well-being of our citizens. Such joint efforts resulted in real change. Our economy has doubled in size. 
Through targeted social policies and international cooperation, 7.5 million people have been lifted out of 
poverty, and 2.7 million citizens are now covered by modern social protection systems. In partnership with 
the UN and our development partners, we have made remarkable progress in promoting gender equality 
and social inclusion — today, women represent 38 percent of the members of Parliament. 
Maternal and child mortality rates have declined, and our ongoing reforms continue to empower families, 
strengthen education and healthcare, and expand opportunities for every citizen. Uzbekistan’s 
achievements have been recognized globally. 
In the Sustainable Development Goals Index, our nation has climbed 19 places to rank 62nd, entering the 
group of the top five fastest-advancing countries in the world. As we now look ahead, we open a new and 
promising chapter in our cooperation with the United Nations — the United Nations Sustainable 
Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) 2026–2030. 
This Framework represents a renewed and strengthened partnership, built on mutual trust, shared 
responsibility, and a common vision for a sustainable and inclusive future. It fully aligns with Uzbekistan’s 
national development strategies, encompassing our key priorities: effective and just governance, improved 
living standards and social protection, quality healthcare and education, environmental protection and 
climate resilience, and the revitalization of the Aral Sea region.
The UNSDCF 2026–2030 is more than a roadmap — it is a shared commitment to unlock the full potential 
of our people and to transform Uzbekistan’s demographic and economic strengths into lasting prosperity. 
It embodies our collective determination to ensure that no one is left behind, that every community benefits 
from progress, and that development is people-centered, equitable, and sustainable. 
As we look toward 2030, we do so with confidence and optimism. Together with our international partners, 
including UN we will continue to build a just, prosperous, and sustainable Uzbekistan — a country where 
opportunity, dignity, and hope are the inheritance of every citizen.
Jamshid Kuchkarov 
Deputy Prime Minister, Minister of Economy and Finance of the Republic of Uzbekistan FOREWORD
Dear people of Uzbekistan,
This new United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework 2026–2030 opens a new 
chapter in our shared journey towards a more inclusive, sustainable, and prosperous Uzbekistan. At its 
heart is a simple promise: to turn the country’s demographic momentum into an opportunity —so that every 
child, young woman and man, and every family can thrive. The main strategic priority is to ensure that all 
people in Uzbekistan can develop their potential and benefit from enhanced well-being, capabilities, and
opportunities in a healthy, sustainable environment in line with the national Sustainable Development 
Goals.
The spirit of this Framework is practical and people-centered. It is about quality schools and clinics that are 
closer to communities; decent jobs and fair social protection that cushion shocks; clean air and water, 
resilient services and green growth; safe spaces and justice that protect rights and dignity; and targeted 
support for the Aral Sea region, to help its communities rebuild livelihoods and hope. The UN will continue 
to be a trusted partner in translating reforms into real improvements in everyday life leaving no one behind. 
Let’s keep moving forward — together, with optimism and determination — to turn Uzbekistan’s human 
potential, young energy, talent and creativity into lasting progress for all. 
Sabine Machl 
United Nations Resident Coordinator in Uzbekistan DECLARATION OF COMMITMENT
The Government of Uzbekistan and the United Nations (UN) are committed to working together to achieve 
the country’s national vision for sustainable development.
The United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (Cooperation Framework) will guide 
the work of the UN system in Uzbekistan until 2030. This framework builds on the successes of our past 
cooperation and represents a joint commitment by the Government of Uzbekistan and the UN system to 
work in close partnership for the achievement of the national priorities framed by the Sustainable 
Development Goals (SDGs) and international human and labour rights commitments. The collective results 
expected from this Cooperation Framework will help the people of Uzbekistan to live longer, healthier, and 
more prosperous and secure lives.
In signing hereafter, the participating partners endorse this Cooperation Framework and underscore their 
joint commitment towards the achievement of its results.
For the Government of Uzbekistan For the United Nations Country Team

Uzbekistan stands at a critical juncture in its 
pursuit of sustainable development. For nearly a 
decade, the country has been transforming through 
widespread structural reforms. Yet, the structural 
transformation remains incomplete, with 
inequalities, governance bottlenecks, and 
environmental vulnerabilities posing significant 
risks to the country’s path to sustainable and 
inclusive development. 
Uzbekistan’s youthful, rapidly growing population 
presents opportunities for economic growth, but 
demographic trends are also straining public 
services and exacerbating regional disparities.
Achieving the nation’s goal of reaching uppermiddle-income status by 2030 will require a 
deepening of reforms to promote inclusive 
economic growth, enhancing governance and 
accountability, and investing in human capital and 
environmental sustainability, ensuring that no one 
is left behind.
This transformation unfolds within a dynamic 
regional context, where Uzbekistan’s role as a 
central node for connectivity and cooperation 
across Central Asia is pivotal. The UN recognizes 
Uzbekistan’s contribution to regional stability and 
economic integration and supports its emorts to 
embed these national reforms within the wider 
framework of regional peace, security, and 
sustainable development.
The Government of Uzbekistan remains committed 
to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Its 
ambitious development plan – the Uzbekistan 2030 
Strategy – includes 100 targets across five priority 
areas that are largely aligned with the SDGs: (i) 
creation of education, healthcare and social 
protection systems that fully meet the needs of the 
population and international standards; (ii) joining 
the ranks of upper-middle-income countries 
through a stable economic growth and decent 
work; (iii) ensuring favourable environmental 
conditions for the population; (iv) creation of a just 
and modern state serving the people; and (v) 
ensuring the sovereignty and security of the 
country.
To support this ambitious agenda, the UN has 
developed a Cooperation Framework (CF) that is 
firmly anchored in the Uzbekistan 2030 Strategy.
Adopting a streamlined approach, the vision for this 
2026-2030 CF is that “By 2030, Uzbekistan 
leverages its demographic dividend and 
implements ambitious reforms, ensuring that all 
people in Uzbekistan can develop their potential 
and benefit from enhanced wellbeing, capabilities, 
and opportunities in a healthy, sustainable 
environment.” To achieve this single, overarching 
priority, the CF is built around six, interlinked 
outcomes: governance and justice, livelihoods and 
social protection, health, education, climate and 
environment, and the Aral Sea Region. 
This CF carries forward the guiding principles from 
the previous framework, which will continue to be 
applied for all interventions undertaken by the UN 
development system: 1) leave no one behind, 2) 
human rights-based approach, 3) gender equality 
and women’s empowerment, 4) accountability, 5) 
sustainability and 6) resilience. Integrated and 
multidimensional programming approach—in line 
with the “five P’s” of the 2030 Agenda (people, 
prosperity, planet, peace and partnerships), will 
guide the process and the content of the UN 
intervention in Uzbekistan.
The CF will be nationally executed under the overall 
coordination of the Ministry of Economy and 
Finance of the Republic of Uzbekistan. It will be 
operationalized through joint work plans developed 
by the UN in collaboration with government 
ministries, state institutions, civil society, and nongovernmental organizations (NGOs). The CF will 
remain responsive to emerging and unforeseen 
needs, and will adapt to significant changes in the 
country context if needed. The UN will establish 
synergies with International Financial Institutions 
(IFIs) and development partners. It will also engage 
with a wide range of national stakeholders including 
media and the private sector. Existing governance 
structures will be revised to align with the new CF, 
ensuring coordinated delivery by the UN system. A 
monitoring, reporting and evaluation plan will be 
implemented in line with UN development system 
standards. The CF will be reviewed and reported 
against annually. It will be evaluated prior to 
subsequent planning cycle.1
CHAPTER 1: COUNTRY PROGRESS TOWARDS THE 2030 AGENDA
Uzbekistan's Development Trajectory: Since 
gaining independence in 1991, Uzbekistan has 
transitioned from a centrally planned economy to a 
market-oriented system, with significant structural 
reforms accelerating under President Shavkat 
Mirziyoyev’s leadership since 2016. These reforms 
aim to elevate the country to the upper-middleincome status by 2030, building on significant GDP 
growth, greater openness, liberalization, elevated 
international commitments, and increasing 
international financial flows. Despite these 
achievements, the structural transformation 
remains incomplete, with inequalities, governance 
bottlenecks, and environmental vulnerabilities 
posing significant risks to the country’s path to 
sustainable and inclusive development. 
Additionally, as a landlocked country surrounded 
only by other landlocked countries, Uzbekistan 
faces connectivity challenges that must be 
overcome to benefit from the international trade, 
and integration into the global economy.
The Government of Uzbekistan remains committed 
to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Its 
ambitious development plan –the Uzbekistan 2030 
Strategy – includes 100 targets across five priority 
areas that are largely aligned with the SDGs: (i) 
creation of education, healthcare and social 
protection systems that fully meet the needs of the 
population and international standards; (ii) joining 
the ranks of upper-middle-income countries 
through a stable economic growth; (iii) ensuring 
favourable environmental conditions for the 
population; (iv) creation of a just and modern state 
serving the people; and (v) ensuring the sovereignty 
and security of the country.
Globally, Uzbekistan has been amongst the 
fastest progressing countries on the SDG Index 
(SDGi) since 2015. In 2025, Uzbekistan ranks 62nd
out of the 193 UN member states covered by the 
index, (Figures 1-4).

Box 1. Harnessing the Demographic Dividend
Uzbekistan’s youthful and rapidly growing 
population offers significant potential for 
bolstering economic growth, social resilience 
and stability. But demographic dividends can 
only be realized if public services, infrastructure 
and employment opportunities keep up with 
demand. The working-age population (15–64 
years) is expected to grow from 23.9 million in 
2024 to over 33 million by 2050.
1 signalling a 
continuation of the "demographic window of 
opportunities" during which a high proportion of 
the working-age population may drive economic 
growth.
These demographic trends are already placing 
immense pressure on public services, 
particularly education, healthcare, and the 
labour market. Urbanization and migration 
trends are also reshaping the demographic 
landscape, highlighting the need for 
infrastructure development in urban areas while 
preventing rural economic stagnation. 
Harnessing the demographic dividend will 
require substantial investments to empower the 
people of Uzbekistan, particularly its young 
population and underserved rural populations 
where disparities are most pronounced. Critical 
needs include improved access to quality and 
inclusive education, vocational training, genderresponsive healthcare and decent jobs. Familyfriendly policies advancing gender equality are 
needed to encourage greater participation of 
women in the workforce. The government must 
also ensure policies and systems can deliver 
services throughout a life course, recognizing the 
emerging trend of population aging. 2

Vulnerable Populations and Social Exclusion: 
Uzbekistan’s 2nd Voluntary National Review (VNR)2
highlights significant achievements regarding the 
situation of vulnerable groups. The country has 
made notable progress on gender equality through 
implementation of a National Strategy for Gender 
Equality, improved access to higher education, and 
adoption of laws to combat violence against 
women. For children, strides have been made in 
enhancing access to early childhood education 
and improving nutrition programs. Reforms for 
people with disabilities, such as inclusive 
education initiatives, and rural development 
programs targeting infrastructure and poverty 
reduction are underway. 
Nevertheless, various population groups in 
Uzbekistan are still at risk of being left behind due 
to a combination of complex factors summarized in 
Box 2 and elaborated further in the Common 
Country Analysis.
3 These include women, children 
and youth in vulnerable situations, people with 
disabilities, people living with HIV, migrants and 
their children, forcibly displaced people, stateless 
persons, and other vulnerable groups. The roots of 
exclusion are multidimensional, driven by 
discriminatory social norms, gender stereotypes, 
regional inequalities, lack of relevant legal 
frameworks and governance deficits. 
Multi-dimensional poverty: According to the 2024 
pilot of the National Multi-dimensional Poverty 
Index (n-MPI), around 18.4 percent of the adult 
population (4.2 million) are multidimensionally 
poor in Uzbekistan as they experience deprivations 
in at least 34 percent of the weighted indicators.4
The main contributors to the multi-dimensional 
poverty5 in the country have been found to be 
Educational attainment (13.7%), Food security 
(11.7%) and Informal employment (11.5%). By 
capturing overlapping deprivations in health, 
education, and living standards, the n-MPI serves 
as a useful complement to income poverty 
measurements for understanding poverty.

The n-MPI revealed stark regional disparities and an 
urban-rural divide in multidimensional poverty. The 
Republic of Karakalpakstan (29.9%), Namangan 
region (27.5%), and Tashkent region (26.5%) having 
the largest proportion of the multidimensionally 
poor. The incidence of multidimensional poverty in 
rural areas is significantly larger (23.2 percent) than 
in urban areas (13.9 percent). This highlights the 
importance of targeted interventions and policies 
that address disparities and cater to the specific 
needs of dimerent areas and vulnerable 
populations. 
Box 2. Main drivers of exclusion
Various population groups in Uzbekistan are still 
at risk of being left behind due to a combination 
of factors related to decent work deficits, 
discrimination, stereotypes, governance, 
legislation, socio-economic status, geography 
and vulnerability to shocks. These groups
experience multiple forms of exclusion that 
intersect, compounding their disadvantages and 
making it difficult for them to fully engage in or 
benefit from the country’s development efforts. 
These patterns of exclusion are not only a 
hindrance to individual well-being, but also pose 
significant challenges to achieving the national 
SDGs.
Social Development – Education, Health, Social 
Protection and Social Services: In recent years, 
Uzbekistan has expanded access to education and 
health services, with significant investments in 
preschool education and Universal Health 
Coverage (UHC). However, the quality of 
education and health services, particularly in rural 
regions, continues to lag behind national goals as 
well as the international benchmarks. For example, 
Uzbekistan scored are amongst the lowest across 
all subjects in the OECD’s Programme for 
International Student Assessment (PISA) in 2022.

fragmentation and empowering the National

Economic Transformation and Inequality: 
Uzbekistan’s economic transformation has 
resulted in robust growth and impressive poverty 
reduction, despite setbacks such as the COVID-19 
pandemic and regional conflicts. However, reforms 
have also been accompanied by rising income 
inequality, driven by high food and energy inflation, 
highly regressive energy subsidies, excessive 
monopolization, fiscal preferences for state-owned 
enterprises (SOEs), and non-transparent
privatization processes. Structural reforms, 
including energy tariff liberalization and the 
privatization of SOEs, need to be more transparent 
and inclusive to avoid exacerbating existing 
inequalities. Addressing informalities in the labour 
market and growing decent employment 
opportunities, especially for women and youth, will 
be key to ensuring broad-based inclusive 
economic growth. Promoting decent jobs requires 
aligning labour market policies with international 
labour standards. This approach advances SDG 8 
while safeguarding fundamental rights at work and 
ensures that employment gains translate into 
sustainable poverty reduction and shared 
prosperity.
These dynamics are further influenced by broader 
regional and global factors – including ongoing 
regional conflicts and sanctions regime, shifting 
trade patterns, climate impacts, and global 
political and economic volatility – which 
underscore the importance of aligning 
Uzbekistan’s economic reforms with regional 
cooperation and international best practices to 
build resilience and foster more equitable growth.
Environmental Sustainability and Climate 
Change: Uzbekistan faces severe environmental 
challenges on its path to sustainable development. 
These are driven by climate change and the Aral 
Sea disaster, as well as the growing population and 
evolving consumption patterns. Water scarcity, 
land degradation, and biodiversity loss threaten 
food security and rural livelihoods, and the wellbeing of vulnerable communities. The crisis in the 
Aral Sea region (Box 3), including its profound 
impacts in Karakalpakstan, has compounded
environmental, economic, and social 
vulnerabilities, underscoring the critical linkages 
between climate resilience and social cohesion as 
well as the importance of regional cooperation.
Air pollution is an increasing cause of concern, 
particularly in large urban settlements such as 
Tashkent and some regional hubs, where it poses 
serious health risk for people, especially children. 
The government's commitment to renewable 
energy and climate resilience, as part of its Paris 
Agreement commitments, is a critical step toward 
a more sustainable future. However, significant 
investments are required to fully address these 
environmental risks and ensure a green, 
participatory and inclusive transition.
Box 3. The Aral Sea Disaster 
Drying of the Aral Sea has led to the creation of a 
vast salt desert - Aralkum, the world’s newest 
desert with the size of more than 5.5 million 
hectares. The salty, toxic dust of the Aralkum 
travels throughout the Aral Sea region and 
beyond, causing substantial economic, food, 
health and environmental insecurities of the 
local population. In recent years, measures have 
been taken to help mitigate this crisis including 
the massive planting of saxauls (shrubs/trees) in 
the dried seabed as well as protective forest 
belts in order to prevent the shifting sand from 
advancing and the spread of dust storms and 
dry, hot winds.
Governance, Rule of Law, and Human Rights: 
Reforms in governance have led to improvements 
in civic space, human rights, women’s political 
participation, and public service delivery (such as
e-governance), alongside a reduction of 
corruption, as evidenced by the country’s 
remarkable progress in relevant global indexes and 
rankings. However, significant gaps remain, 
especially in enforcing laws and accountability, 
and civic space remains restricted. Ensuring 
transparent governance and further reduction of 
corruption, particularly in areas such as 5
restructuring of SOEs and social service delivery –
notably in health and education sectors – will be 
essential for achieving the national SDGs at all 
levels (including provincial and mahalla levels).
Uzbekistan’s development financing is
characterized by a blend of public and private
financing mechanisms, innovative financial 
instruments such as SDG and Green bonds, and 
increased engagement with the private sector, IFIs 
and donors. The integrated national financing 
framework (INFF) and Integrated National SDG 
Financing Strategy reflect the country’s 
commitment to aligning financial flows with its 
development priorities. In this regard, Uzbekistan’s 
approach is consistent with the principles of the 
Sevilla Outcome Document on Financing for 
Development (2025),
7 which calls for strengthening 
integrated national financing frameworks, 
mobilizing long-term sustainable financing, and 
enhancing the coherence and effectiveness of 
development cooperation to achieve the SDGs. In 
line with these commitments, Uzbekistan seeks to 
leverage its reform momentum to mobilize 
resources – both public and private, domestic and 
external – more effectively for inclusive, green and

Achievement of the strategic priority of the CF is

Box 12. Harmonized Approach to Cash Transfer (HACT)
The HACT framework represents a common operational (harmonized) framework for transferring cash to 
government and non-governmental Implementation Partners (IPs), irrespective of whether these partners 
work with one or multiple United Nation agencies. The objective of the HACT framework is to support a 
closer alignment of development aid with national priorities and to strengthen national capacities for 
management and accountability, with the ultimate objective of gradually shifting to national systems. It 
is understood that ‘harmonized’ in the context of the HACT framework refers to agencies implementing a 
common operational framework using the same, consistent, standardized approach and tools to 
manage financial risks in a coordinated fashion.
The Harmonized Cash Transfer (HACT)-specific mechanisms apply only to those UN system agencies 
that follow HACT procedures.
All cash transfers to an Implementing Partner are based on the Work Plans (WPs)28 agreed between the
Implementing Partner and the UN system agencies.
Cash transfers for activities detailed in work plans (WPs) can be made by the UN system agencies using
the following modalities:
1. Cash transferred directly to the Implementing Partner:
a. Prior to the start of activities (direct cash transfer), or
b. After activities have been completed (reimbursement);
2. Direct payment to vendors or third parties for obligations incurred by the Implementing Partners on the 
basis of requests signed by the designated official of the Implementing Partner;

of activities agreed with Implementing Partners.
Where cash transfers are made to the State Treasury, the State Treasury shall transfer such cash 
promptly to the Implementing Partner.
Direct cash transfers shall be requested and released for programme implementation periods not
exceeding three months. Reimbursements of previously authorized expenditures shall be requested and
released quarterly or after the completion of activities. The UN system agencies shall not be obligated to 
reimburse expenditure made by the Implementing Partner over and above the authorized amounts.

Cash transfer modalities, the size of disbursements, and the scope and frequency of assurance activities

4.1. MONITORING PLAN
The national SDG indicator framework, aligned with 
the global SDG indicators, is the basis for 
establishing the Cooperation Framework (CF)
outcome indicators. The indicators at Tier I for 
which metadata and data are available and at Tier II 
for which metadata are available but not collected
will be used to establish key performance 
indicators, baselines, and targets. Given that the 
outcome indicators are drawn from the national
SDG indicator framework, the outcome
performance monitoring will be conducted in close 
coordination with the inter-agency working group 
on national SDG indicators set up by government 
under the Roadmap for national SDG

the implementation of outcomes, agencies report 
on output indicators aligned with the UN’s global 
output indicator framework.
Data collection instruments and sources expected 
to be used for measuring progress at outcome level
will include UN Common Country Analysis, 
government-commissioned data generation 
activities (including census, surveys, the SDG 
Voluntary National Reviews), national reports to

recommendations and concluding observations of 
the UN Treaty Bodies, UPR Working Group reports

partners.
Monitoring of the CF will take place throughout the 
entire implementation phase and serve as an 
action-learning process to ensure continuous 
testing, learning, and adaption. To this end, the MEL 
experts, in coordination with the Results Groups, 
will actively track progress towards planned results, 
monitor changes, and identify emerging 
opportunities and risks. Refinements and 
adjustments will be made iteratively based on 
learning gained through analysis, evaluations and 
other sources of evidence and data collection.
Key mechanisms for CF monitoring will include:
• CF Annual Review and reporting, including 
through the UNINFO data portal.
• UN entity monitoring and evaluation activities.
• UN entities’ joint monitoring of joint 
programmes and projects.
• Quarterly meetings of the Results Groups, with 
engagement of MEL experts.

submitted to the Joint Steering Committee. The 
report will focus on the progress in achieving the 
CF’s priorities, outcomes, and outputs, through 
collection and analysis of data by the agency MEL 
experts using UNINFO and Results Groups. 
Furthermore, it will examine new opportunities or 
changes in the external context that might require 
expansion or contraction of the UN’s 
priorities/programmes. It will also assess the 
overall implementation quality, operational 
delivery, resource mobilization performance, and 
partnerships that are critical for CF delivery.

annual review meeting at which the UN Resident 
Coordinator, on behalf of the UNCT, will present the 
Country Results Report to government and 
stakeholders. The annual review meeting can be 
extended to invite representatives of development 
partners, civil society, and youth to ensure the 
widest possible engagement the joint UN and 
government cooperation for development. During 
the review, the Joint Steering Committee co-chairs 
will determine if formal revisions of the CF are 
required and recommend changes to be made.

updated yearly to feed into the annual review. To

An independent evaluation, which contributes to 
system-wide oversight, transparency, 
accountability, and collective learning, should be 
completed in the penultimate year of the CF. The 
evaluation will adhere to the United Nations 
Evaluation Group (UNEG) Norms and Standards 
and aim to reflect the evaluation indicators in the 
Funding Compact, the UN-SWAP and the United 
Nation Disability Inclusion Strategy. Linkages 
should be made with individual and joint UN 
agency-level evaluations as well as National 
Voluntary Reviews of SDGs to maximize 
complementarities. Moreover, using the UN CCA as 
a benchmark, the evaluation should also assess 
whether expected results were achieved, if other 
unintended results are observed, and whether the

cost-emicient contribution to national development 
priorities.

manner and promote national ownership through 
meaningful engagement of national partners

other development partners (including IFIs). Based 
on the findings and recommendations, an 
evaluation management response and action plan 
will be prepared by the UNCT. The final evaluation 
will be publicly disclosed and inform the visioning 
exercise, theories of change, and the strategic 
prioritization of subsequent CFs.
